newsitem.title: CHILE: Minas Gerais to sell one-third Cemig by December.
newsitem.headline: Minas Gerais to sell one-third Cemig by December.

text.p: The government of Minas Gerais will sell one third of state electrical company Cemig by early December as part of a sweeping privatization program in banking and energy, officials of the Brazilian state said.

After the Cemig sale, the state will privatize two banks, a natural gas company and a few smaller holdings, all by the middle of 1997, said officials who came to Chile to try to tempt Chilean investors into bidding.
"Our aim is to diminish the state's size to attend better the people's needs," said Minas Gerais Governor Eduardo Azeredo, leading a large trade delegation.
Chilean firms Chilectra SA and its parent company Empresa Nacional de Electricidad SA or Endesa Chile had both expressed interest in bidding for the 33 percent share of Cemig, said officials.

The official announcement and terms of the Cemig sale will be made by October 31, and the state plans to auction it off by late November or early December, said Deputy Governor Waldrifo Silvino dos Mares Guia.
With 5,000 MW capacity -- about the same as all Chile -- and five million customers, Cemig is currently owned 84 percent by the state.
The state's share will fall to 51 percent after the sale, said dos Mares.
"The state is not interested in total privatization of Cemig...precisely because it's a profitable concern," he said. "And we don't want to sell to several buyers. We want a strategic partner."
The state is now ready to sell Banco Credito Real, with its 83 branch offices, within the next 100 days, said dos Mares.
After that, it will seek legislative approval to sell much larger Banco do Estado de Minas Gerais (BEMG) early next year, he said. The bank has over 300 branch offices throughout Brazil.
"We don't want the state to be in the banking industry any more. We have other priorities," said dos Mares. Sale of state gas company Gasmig will follow, sometime in mid-1997, he said.
Chilean firms have been looking at a host of Brazilian power privatizations, deciding which to bid on and which to pass up.

Most are in markets more familiar to Chileans than Minas Gerais, such as Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro, but dos Mares denied he would have to fight other states for potential bidders. "Cemig is profitable and well-managed, so we don't see any competition with other big companies," he said.
Apart from the Chilean firms, "four or five others" had shown interest in bidding for Cemig, he said.

Chilean power firms are pushing fast into Latin American markets. Endesa Chile, owned about 25 percent by Enersis SA, has major holdings in Peru and Argentina and announced Tuesday it would bid in power privatizations in Colombia and Mexico.
